Low-Carbon Calypso

A steel pan that plays one chromatic octave, built from flat sheet steel, with a pair of mallets turned to match.

Brief

I’m part of Cardinal Calypso at Stanford, and I wanted to play an instrument I made myself. The goal was a working steel pan in three parts: a bowl with the notes hammered into it, a rolled skirt, and two mallets. The stand is borrowed from the group.

CAD

I modeled the bowl with its note layout, the skirt, the mallets, and the full assembly. Modeling every part also made me think through how I would make each one.

A setback

My first idea was to press the bowl into shape with a mold in the hydraulic press. It didn’t work: the sheet wrinkled instead of forming a smooth dish. I dropped the press and decided to form the bowl by hammering.

Mallets

With the press idea stalled, I moved to the lathe and turned the mallet handles from aluminum rod. After turning to final diameter and facing the ends, I sanded the handles and fitted rubber heads.

Bowl

I cut a circular blank on the waterjet and annealed it so it would move under the hammer. Then came the longest step: hammering the blank into a bowl and the note bubbles into it. A finger brake formed the flat rim around the edge.

Skirt and joining

I slip-rolled a flat sheet into the skirt. Hammering left the bowl’s edge uneven and its diameter hard to match, so I made a saddle plate with an adjustable diameter. It lets the bowl overhang the skirt by a flexible amount. With the pieces fitted, I TIG welded the bowl and skirt together. During the weld, the overhang melted down to fill the gaps.

Finishing and results

I hammered in the notes, tuned the pan, and then sanded down the entire thing. It plays, but it needs more tuning before it goes to rehearsals and gigs with Calypso.

This was a hard project with a lot of setbacks. The biggest were the failed press mold and welding a hammered bowl to a rolled skirt. Pan making and tuning is a craft of its own, and I came away with fabrication skills that carry over to other work. I learned so much from this project, and I’m extremely happy with the outcome.
